title: Bases and dimension
objectives: Prove that every basis has the same length, and extend an independent list to a basis.

screens.title: Coordinates in a new basis
screens.prose: $(1, x - 1, (x - 1)^2)$ is a basis of $\mathcal{P}_2(\mathbb{R})$. Write $p(x) = 3 + 2x + x^2$ as $a + b(x - 1) + c(x - 1)^2$. The sliders start at the coefficients of $p$ in $(1, x, x^2)$. Move them until the curves match.
screens.question: What is $(a, b, c)$?

hints.text: At $x = 1$ only $a$ survives, so $a = p(1)$.
$p(1) = 6$. Then match the $x^2$ and $x$ terms.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Put $x = 1$ to find $a$, then compare the $x^2$ and $x$ terms.

byKey.std: You kept the coefficients in $(1, x, x^2)$. In this basis they draw $x^2 + 2$, which is $p - 1$.
byKey.length: Your answer has the wrong number of entries. It needs 3, one per coordinate.

explain.text: At $x = 1$ the curve reads $a$, and $p(1) = 6$. The $x^2$ coefficient gives $c = 1$, and then the $x$ terms give $b - 2 = 2$, so $b = 4$. Check: $6 + 4x - 4 + x^2 - 2x + 1 = x^2 + 2x + 3$.

screens.title: How many settings work?
screens.prose: Keep moving the sliders. Look for a second setting of $(a, b, c)$ that also lands exactly on the dashed curve.

We fixed one basis here, $(1, x - 1, (x - 1)^2)$. In it, the setting is unique.

explain.text: Every change of $(a, b, c)$ moves the curve, because the basis is independent. So each polynomial has one set of coordinates. Next we prove it for any basis.

screens.title: Coordinates are unique
screens.prose: A **basis** of $V$ is a list that is independent and spans $V$. Spanning gives every $\mathbf{v}$ at least one set of coordinates. Prove there is only one. Write $[\mathbf{v}]_{\mathcal{B}}$ for the coordinate vector in basis $\mathcal{B}$.
screens.question: Put the lines in order. One line does not belong: move it to Left out.

lines.text: Let $(\mathbf{v}_1, \dots, \mathbf{v}_n)$ be a basis and $\mathbf{v} = a_1\mathbf{v}_1 + \dots + a_n\mathbf{v}_n$ $= c_1\mathbf{v}_1 + \dots + c_n\mathbf{v}_n$.
The list is independent, so every $a_k - c_k = 0$.
So $a_k = c_k$ for every $k$: the coordinates are unique. $\blacksquare$
The list spans $V$, so every $a_k - c_k = 0$.
lines.why: Spanning gives existence. It is independence that forces the weights to be zero.

hints.text: Take two sets of coordinates for one vector.
Subtract the two representations.
Two ways; subtract; independence; equal.

feedback.correct: Right. Two representations differ by a combination giving $\mathbf{0}$, so they agree.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write $\mathbf{v}$ two ways, subtract, then use independence.

byKey.x1: You used spanning to kill the weights. Spanning says nothing about zero combinations; independence does.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs.

explain.text: Two coordinate lists give a combination equal to $\mathbf{0}$. Independence makes every weight $a_k - c_k$ zero. So $[p]_{\mathcal{B}} = (6, 4, 1)$ is the only answer for the hook.

screens.title: Every basis has the same length
screens.prose: `elimination` l7 stated without proof that every basis of a space has the same size. Axler 2.34 proves it from the last lesson's theorem.
screens.question: Put the lines in order. One line does not belong: move it to Left out.

lines.text: Let $B_1$ and $B_2$ be bases of a finite-dimensional $V$.
$B_1$ is independent and $B_2$ spans $V$, so $\operatorname{len} B_1 \le \operatorname{len} B_2$, by Axler 2.22.
$B_2$ is independent and $B_1$ spans $V$, so $\operatorname{len} B_2 \le \operatorname{len} B_1$, by Axler 2.22.
$B_1$ and $B_2$ both span $V$, so they have the same length.
lines.why: Two spanning lists can differ in length: $(\mathbf{e}_1, \mathbf{e}_2)$ and $(\mathbf{e}_1, \mathbf{e}_2, \mathbf{e}_1 + \mathbf{e}_2)$ both span $\mathbb{R}^2$.

hints.text: Use Axler 2.22 twice.
Each basis is independent, and each spans.
Name the bases; $\le$ one way; $\le$ the other way; equal.

feedback.correct: Right. Two inequalities, one each way, give equality.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Apply Axler 2.22 with $B_1$ independent and $B_2$ spanning, then the other way round.

byKey.x1: You used spanning alone. Lists that span can have any length above the dimension.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs.

explain.text: Axler 2.22 needs one independent list and one spanning list. Each basis can play either part. So the lengths bound each other, and they are equal.

screens.title: Why we may swap
screens.prose: Line 3 runs Axler 2.22 again with $B_1$ and $B_2$ in swapped roles.
screens.question: Why are we allowed to swap them?

options.text: Both lists are independent and both span $V$.

options.why: It is not: $2 \le 3$ but $3 \not\le 2$. The swap needs a fact about the lists.

options.text: Because $B_1$ and $B_2$ hold the same vectors.
options.why: They need not. $(\mathbf{e}_1, \mathbf{e}_2)$ and $((1, 1), (1, -1))$ are different bases of $\mathbb{R}^2$.
That makes the lengths finite, but the swap needs each list to play both roles.

hints.text: Axler 2.22 needs an independent list and a spanning list.
What does "basis" give us about each list?
Each basis is both independent and spanning.

feedback.correct: Right. A basis is both, so either can play either role.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Recall what a basis is.

explain.text: A basis is independent and spanning. So $B_2$ can be the independent list and $B_1$ the spanning one. That gives the second inequality.

screens.title: Dimension
screens.prose: The **dimension** $\dim V$ is the length of any basis. For $p(1) = 0$, try $x - 1$, $x^2 - 1$, $x^3 - 1$: each vanishes at 1. Every $p$ with $p(1) = 0$ is $p - p(1) \cdot 1$, a combination of them.

rows: the six matrices with one entry 1

screens.question: Fill in each dimension.

hints.text: Count the vectors in a basis.
$\mathcal{P}_3$ has $1, x, x^2, x^3$: four. The $p(1) = 0$ space has three listed.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the vectors in each basis.

byKey.r1c1: You counted the degree. $\mathcal{P}_3$ has the four basis vectors $1, x, x^2, x^3$.
byKey.r3c1: You counted all of $\mathcal{P}_3$. The condition $p(1) = 0$ cuts one dimension: $x - 1, x^2 - 1, x^3 - 1$.
byKey.r4c1: You counted the vector $\mathbf{0}$. Its basis is the empty list, of length 0.

explain.text: $\dim \mathbb{F}^n = n$, $\dim \mathcal{P}_m = m + 1$ and $\dim \mathbb{F}^{m \times n} = mn$. The three polynomials $x - 1, x^2 - 1, x^3 - 1$ have different degrees, so they are independent. $\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{F})$ has no finite basis, so it is infinite-dimensional.

screens.title: Extend to a basis
screens.prose: Axler 2.31: add $\mathbf{e}_1, \mathbf{e}_2, \dots$ in turn, keeping each one not in the span so far. Start from $\mathbf{v}_1 = (1, 0, 1, 0)$, $\mathbf{v}_2 = (0, 1, 0, 1)$ in $\mathbb{R}^4$. Reducing a spanning list (Axler 2.30) works the same way, dropping instead.
screens.question: Keep or skip each $\mathbf{e}_j$?

hints.text: A vector of $\operatorname{span}(\mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2)$ has the form $(a, b, a, b)$.
$\mathbf{e}_1$ is not of that form. Then $(\mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2, \mathbf{e}_1)$ gives $(a + c, b, a, b)$, which misses $\mathbf{e}_2$.
Keep, keep, then four vectors span $\mathbb{R}^4$: skip, skip.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. For each $\mathbf{e}_j$, ask whether it is a combination of the vectors kept so far.

byKey.r2c1: You kept $\mathbf{e}_3$. With four independent vectors kept, the list already spans $\mathbb{R}^4$: $\mathbf{e}_3 = \mathbf{v}_1 - \mathbf{e}_1$.
byKey.r3c1: You kept $\mathbf{e}_4$. It is $\mathbf{v}_2 - \mathbf{e}_2$, already in the span.

explain.text: $\mathbf{e}_1$ and $\mathbf{e}_2$ each add a direction, giving four independent vectors in $\mathbb{R}^4$. Then $\mathbf{e}_3 = \mathbf{v}_1 - \mathbf{e}_1$ and $\mathbf{e}_4 = \mathbf{v}_2 - \mathbf{e}_2$ are skipped. In $\mathbb{R}^3$, $(1, 1, 0), (0, 1, 1)$ keeps only $\mathbf{e}_1$, as in the exchange.

screens.title: The right length is enough
screens.prose: Let $\dim V = n$. A list of length $n$ need only pass one test: independent, or spanning. Take the independent case.
screens.question: Why is an independent list of length $n$ a basis?

options.text: Extend it to a basis. Every basis has length $n$, so nothing was added.

options.why: $(\mathbf{e}_1)$ is independent in $\mathbb{R}^2$ and spans only a line.
That is the claim itself. The proof must say why.

options.text: Reduce it to a basis by removing vectors.
options.why: Reduction applies to spanning lists. An independent list is extended, not reduced.

hints.text: Axler 2.31 extends an independent list to a basis.
The extended list has length $\dim V = n$.
It started at length $n$, so nothing was added.

feedback.correct: Right. Extending adds nothing, so the list was already a basis.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Extend the list to a basis and count.

explain.text: Extension gives a basis containing the list, of length $n$ by Axler 2.34. The list already has length $n$, so nothing was added. A spanning list of length $n$ is a basis the same way, by reduction.

screens.title: Dimension of a sum
screens.prose: For subspaces $U$ and $W$ of a finite-dimensional space, $$\dim(U + W) = \dim U + \dim W - \dim(U \cap W).$$ The intersection is counted twice, so subtract it once. Take $U = \operatorname{span}\{(1, 0, 1, 0), (0, 1, 0, 1)\}$ and $W = \operatorname{span}\{(1, 1, 0, 0), (0, 0, 1, 1)\}$. They meet in $\operatorname{span}\{(1, 1, 1, 1)\}$.
screens.question: What is $\dim(U + W)$?

hints.text: $\dim U = \dim W = 2$.
$\dim(U \cap W) = 1$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use $\dim U + \dim W - \dim(U \cap W)$.

byKey.add: You added the dimensions and ignored the overlap. $(1, 1, 1, 1)$ is in both, so subtract 1.
byKey.int: You gave $\dim(U \cap W)$. The question asks for the sum.

explain.text: $(a, b, a, b) = (c, c, d, d)$ forces all four equal, so $U \cap W = \operatorname{span}\{(1, 1, 1, 1)\}$. Then $\dim(U + W) = 2 + 2 - 1 = 3$. The homework proves the formula.

screens.title: Count the vectors?
screens.prose: We are given $\mathbf{a} = (1, 0, 1, 0)$, $\mathbf{b} = (0, 1, 0, 1)$ and $\mathbf{c} = (1, 1, 1, 1)$. A classmate says $\dim \operatorname{span}(\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c}) = 3$, one per vector.
screens.question: What is $\dim \operatorname{span}(\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c})$?

hints.text: Is one vector a combination of the others?
Add $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$.
$\mathbf{c} = \mathbf{a} + \mathbf{b}$, so $(\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b})$ is a basis of the span.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Reduce the list to a basis first, then count.

byKey.count: You counted the vectors given. $\mathbf{c} = \mathbf{a} + \mathbf{b}$ adds no new direction.
byKey.amb: You gave the dimension of $\mathbb{R}^4$. The span is smaller than the whole space.

explain.text: $\mathbf{c} = \mathbf{a} + \mathbf{b}$, so reduction drops $\mathbf{c}$. $(\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b})$ is independent, so it is a basis of the span. Dimension counts a basis, not the list we were handed.

screens.title: Extend in code
screens.prose: The extension algorithm decides "in the span so far" by rank: adding $\mathbf{e}_j$ either raises the dimension by 1 or leaves it. Vectors are lists, given as rows. A dependent input has no basis to extend, so raise `ValueError`.
screens.question: Complete `dim_span(vectors)` and `extend_to_basis(vectors, n)`.

widget.starter:
import numpy as np

def dim_span(vectors):
    # the rank of the matrix with these rows (0 for an empty list)
    return None

def extend_to_basis(vectors, n):
    out = [list(v) for v in vectors]
    # raise ValueError if out is dependent
    # then try e_1, ..., e_n in turn, keeping each that raises the dimension
    return None
widget.how: Check runs 10 hidden tests: lists compared exactly, whole numbers, and two inputs that must raise `ValueError`. The first run loads NumPy, which takes a few seconds.

hints.text: `dim_span` is `np.linalg.matrix_rank` of the rows, with 0 for an empty list.
In `extend_to_basis`, compare `dim_span(out)` with `len(out)` to spot a dependent input.
Loop `j` over `range(n)`, build `e`, and append it when `dim_span(out + [e]) > len(out)`.

feedback.correct: Right. Greedy extension by rank gives the bases we found by hand.
feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Read the first failing row: is it the dependence check, the empty list, or the order of the kept vectors?

byKey.test-6: A dependent input such as $(1, 2), (2, 4)$ must raise `ValueError` before any extension.
byKey.test-4: The empty list is independent, so it extends to all of $\mathbf{e}_1, \dots, \mathbf{e}_n$.
byKey.error: Your code stopped with an error. Check the empty-list case in `dim_span`.

explain.text:
`dim_span` is the rank. A list is independent exactly when its rank equals its length, so that is the `ValueError` test. Each $\mathbf{e}_j$ is kept when it raises the rank.

```python

    out.append(e)
```

screens.title: How many bets?
screens.prose: Six days of yield-curve moves, in basis points, at four maturities. Each day is a vector in $\mathbb{R}^4$. They were built from a level factor $(1, 1, 1, 1)$ and a slope factor $(-3, -1, 1, 3)$. The weights are not given.
screens.question: What is the dimension of the span of the six daily moves?

hints.text: Every day is a combination of the two factors.
So the span lies inside $\operatorname{span}\{(1, 1, 1, 1), (-3, -1, 1, 3)\}$.
Day 3 is level alone and day 4 is slope alone, so both factors are reached: dimension 2.

feedback.correct: Right. Six days, but only two independent bets: level and slope.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask how many directions the six rows really use.

byKey.days: You counted the days. Every day is a combination of two factors.
byKey.mats: You counted the maturities. The moves use only two directions of $\mathbb{R}^4$.

explain.text: Day 3 is $3 \times$ level and day 4 is $-1 \times$ slope, so both factors lie in the span. Every other day is a combination of them. So the rank is 2: a level bet and a slope bet, as in `eigen` l12.

ideas: A basis is an independent spanning list. Each vector has exactly one coordinate vector in it.
Every basis of a finite-dimensional space has the same length, $\dim V$: Axler 2.22 applied both ways.
An independent list extends to a basis, and a spanning list reduces to one. In dimension $n$, either kind of length $n$ is already a basis.

quiz.prose: $\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{F})$ holds every polynomial. Each $\mathcal{P}_m(\mathbb{F})$ sits inside it.
quiz.question: What can we say about $\dim \mathcal{P}(\mathbb{F})$?

options.text: It has no finite basis: it is infinite-dimensional.

options.why: That is $\dim \mathcal{P}_m$. No single $m$ caps every polynomial.

options.text: It is 0, since there is no finite basis.
options.why: Dimension 0 belongs to $\{\mathbf{0}\}$, with the empty basis.

options.text: It is the number of polynomials.
options.why: Dimension counts a basis, not the vectors in the space.

feedback.correct: Right. $(1, x, \dots, x^m)$ is independent for every $m$, so no finite list can span.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare with independent lists $(1, x, \dots, x^m)$.
